home.title: The HEKA Calendar
home.hook: Time is the structure we live inside. What if it fit better?

ch1.title: What Is HEKA?
ch1.hook: A calendar is more than a counting system. It is the rhythm of your life.

ch2.title: The Shape of a Year
ch2.hook: April begins. March closes. Everything in between makes sense.

ch3.title: Living in HEKA
ch3.hook: You do not need permission to use a better tool.

ch4.title: The Two Modes
ch4.hook: One calendar. Two ways of honoring the sun. You choose.

ch5.title: The Calendar Revolution
ch5.hook: Gregorian was a patch. HEKA is a redesign.

ch6.title: Start Using HEKA Today
ch6.hook: No institutions need to change. Only your view.

ch7.title: Time That Serves You
ch7.hook: The calendar you use shapes the life you live.

0.b: Irregular months. Scattered holidays. A year that stumbles from January to December with no sense of beginning, middle, or end. You have felt this friction. HEKA removes it.

1.b: Thirteen months. Twelve have twenty-eight days in perfect symmetry. March, the closing month, carries the leap day. Four perfect weeks per month. A year that flows: April opens, May through December form the stable core, January through March complete it.

2.b: HEKA does not disrupt your life. Civil dates remain visible. Your appointments, commitments, and legal obligations stay exactly where they are. You simply gain a clearer lens.

0.b: April is the threshold. The year does not begin in winter exhaustion, but in spring vitality. New growth. New projects. The opening announces: something is beginning.

1.b: May through December is the long, stable middle. Nine months of perfectly regular and predictable rhythm. Plan with confidence. Build momentum. This is where the work happens.

2.b: January through March bring the year to its resolution. Finish what you started. Harvest what you grew. Closure creates space for reflection and prepares you for the next opening.

0.b: Activate the civil overlay and see Gregorian dates alongside HEKA. Your dentist appointment, your mother's birthday, your tax deadline -- everything stays exactly where you expect.

1.b: Save thoughts by day or by month. Print clean monthly views or full-year panoramas. The calendar becomes a journal, a planner, a record of your days.

2.b: Moon phases appear instantly. Track the lunar rhythm alongside your HEKA dates. Optional, elegant, there when you want it.

0.b: March gains its extra day when the Gregorian calendar says so. For daily coordination with the civil world, this is your mode. Same structure. Familiar time.

1.b: HEKA follows its own correction rule: every fourth year has a 30-day March, except every 128 years which does not. This is astronomical precision. This is long-term integrity.

2.b: The months do not change. The week does not change. Only the correction trigger shifts. Experiment. See which mode fits your needs. You are not trapped.

0.b: Our current calendar is a pile of historical accidents. Roman politics. Religious councils. Astronomical patches added centuries apart. It was never designed as a system.

1.b: 1582: Pope Gregory fixed the drift problem. But he kept the irregular months, the scattered structure, the inherited chaos. A necessary correction, but not a complete solution.

2.b: We keep what works: seven-day weeks, seasonal alignment, solar year tracking. We redesign what does not: month structure, yearly flow, correction placement. Built for minds that think.

0.b: Activate civil dates. Now you see both systems simultaneously. Your HEKA date and your Gregorian date. The bridge is built. Cross when you need to.

1.b: Start with SYNC if you want familiarity. Switch to TRUE if you want purity. You can change your mind. The calendar adapts to you, not the other way around.

2.b: Use HEKA as your main view. Plan your month. Note your days. Feel the difference of a year with real structure. The civil world does not need to know. You will know.

0.b: Every time you wonder how many days are in this month, you pay a small tax. Every irregularity drains focus. HEKA removes these taxes. You keep your energy for what matters.

1.b: When structure is predictable, the mind relaxes. You know where you are in the year. You feel the opening, the core, the closing. Time becomes a space you inhabit, not a chaos you survive.

2.b: You did not choose the Gregorian calendar. It was given to you. HEKA is a choice. To use a tool designed for clarity. To reclaim agency over the structure of your days. This is your calendar.

0.t: Is this a religion or movement?
0.b: Neither. HEKA is a tool. Like a better hammer or a clearer map.

1.b: Twelve months of irregular length force mental gymnastics. Thirteen months of four weeks each creates perfect regularity. 13 x 28 = 364. Plus one special day. The math is clean. The experience is cleaner.

2.b: You see HEKA dates. They see civil dates. When you say "March 15th," you mean the same day they do. The civil overlay ensures you never lose coordination. You gain clarity. They lose nothing.

0.t: Why does the year start in April?
0.b: Spring is the universal opening. Growth begins. Energy rises. Beginning the year in April aligns the calendar with the felt experience of renewal. January starts in winter exhaustion. April starts in spring possibility.

1.b: April, May, June, July, August, Hexa, September, October, November, December, January, February, March. Hexa -- the sixth month -- fills the gap. The rest you already know. Only their positions change.

2.b: Every solar calendar needs correction. HEKA places it all in March, at the year's end. March has 29 days, or 30 in leap years. The other twelve months are perfect and permanently regular. Correction is contained, not scattered.

0.b: Yes. Print monthly views or full-year panoramas. Clean, clear, designed for paper. Put them on walls. Carry them in notebooks. Digital convenience and physical artifact, both.

1.b: Activate holiday sets for your region. Or ignore them. HEKA does not impose its own holidays; it helps you follow the ones that matter to you, overlaid on a clearer structure.

2.b: Everything is stored locally on your device. Your thoughts remain yours. Export them if you wish. Import them elsewhere. You control your data completely.

0.b: Both. SYNC is correct for coordination with the civil world. TRUE is correct for astronomical precision. Your needs determine which correction is more important to you right now.

1.t: Does TRUE mode drift from civil dates?
1.b: Slowly, yes. TRUE mode follows its own leap year rule, not the Gregorian one. Over centuries, the divergence becomes noticeable. For daily life, the difference is imperceptible. For long-term thinking, purity matters.

2.b: Eventually, perhaps. But institutions do not need to change for you to benefit. HEKA works perfectly as a personal overlay. Start there. Let the tool prove itself.

0.t: Why do months have different lengths?
0.b: Roman politics. Julius Caesar and Augustus needed months named in their honor. The calendar was adjusted to accommodate egos. These irregularities became 'tradition.' Tradition is not always wisdom.

1.b: It fixed the drift. It did not fix the structure. Months remained irregular, quarters remained unequal, the year had no narrative shape. A necessary patch, but not a fundamental redesign.

2.b: Many. The French Republican calendar. The World Calendar. The International Fixed Calendar. Some brilliant, all politically failed. HEKA learns from them: civil time compatibility is essential. Revolution through evolution.

0.t: How do I explain this to others?
0.b: You do not need to. Use it. If they ask, say: "I found a calendar that helps me plan better." Show them. Let them see the clarity. Persuasion happens through demonstration, not declaration.

1.t: What if I want to stop using it?
1.b: Stop using it. Your civil dates remain. Your appointments stay where they are. No lock-in. No sunk cost. HEKA must earn its place in your life every day, or it does not deserve to stay.

2.t: Where do I begin right now?
2.b: Open settings. Activate the civil overlay. Look at today in both systems. That is the first step. You have already taken it by opening this guide.

0.t: Does the calendar really affect mindset?
0.b: Deeply. We think in the structures we inhabit. Irregular months create low-level cognitive friction. Regular months create cognitive flow. You may not notice the friction until it disappears. Then you cannot stop noticing it.

1.b: Keep them. Your birthday. Your New Year celebrations. Your seasonal festivals. HEKA does not erase culture; it provides a clearer container for it. The content remains. The container improves.

2.t: Why is this important enough to build?
2.b: Because time is the substrate of life. Because we deserve tools designed for minds, not inherited from accidents. Because someone should try to build something better. We did. You are here.

chapterLeads.ch1: You have felt it. The slight confusion when planning across months. The mental calculation: "How many days until...?" The irregular rhythm of a year that stumbles from January through December with no coherent shape. HEKA is the response.
chapterLeads.ch2: A year is not merely a count of days. It is a narrative arc. HEKA structures the solar year into three distinct movements: the Opening, the Core, and the Closing. Each with its own character. Each serving a different purpose in the rhythm of work and rest, growth and harvest.
chapterLeads.ch3: Theory becomes useful only when practiced. HEKA is designed for immediate adoption without disruption. Civil dates remain visible. Your appointments stay synchronized. You simply gain a clearer, more regular framework for navigating your days.
chapterLeads.ch4: Every solar calendar must correct for the mismatch between day-cycles and year-cycles. HEKA offers two approaches to this correction: one that harmonizes with civil expectations, and one that follows pure astronomical precision. The structure stays constant. Only the correction mechanism changes.
chapterLeads.ch5: The Gregorian calendar is not bad. It is a successful standard that fixed critical drift problems. But it is also a patch on a patch—a structure shaped by Roman politics, religious councils, and historical accidents rather than human needs. Understanding this history clarifies why redesign is worth attempting.
chapterLeads.ch6: Institutional change is slow. Personal change is immediate. You do not need governments or corporations to adopt HEKA for you to benefit from it. Start today. Use it as your personal planning layer. Let the tool prove its value in your own experience.
chapterLeads.ch7: We live inside our calendars. They shape our sense of time, progress, and possibility. An irregular calendar creates low-level friction throughout the year. A regular calendar creates flow. The choice of which structure to inhabit is ultimately a choice about what kind of temporal environment you want to live within.
